why.summary: Allergy travelers cannot tell what is safe to order from a menu they cannot read

ratings.rationale: For a traveler with celiac disease or a nut allergy, every restaurant meal abroad is a risk decision. The user eats out 2 to 3 times a day on a trip and reports skipping meals or eating only packaged food on past trips. One bad dish costs a day of the trip.

Google Lens translates words literally: it renders a dish name but not what is in it. Printed allergy cards get a nod from staff who do not read them carefully. Asking the waiter fails across the language barrier. Three linked r/Celiac threads describe the same pattern.

Hypothesis: a one-trip pass at 4.99 USD or 19.99 USD a year. The allergy traveler already spends on cards and apps. Cost per trip estimated at roughly 0.14 USD in model calls (see ASM-002). Willingness to pay is untested.

Success: at least 60 percent of scans end with the user tapping "I ordered this" within the session. Kill signal: under 20 percent after the first 200 users, or more than two reports of a flagged dish that was unsafe.

caps.reason: Cleared in turn 2: workarounds named with their failure

who.summary: Beachhead under review: vegetarians and vegans abroad proposed at turn 12, replacing allergy travelers

ratings.rationale: The new segment is named but its context, workflow and the moment the product appears are not yet described. PERSONA-001 describes the old segment.
The allergy trigger and objections do not transfer. Vegans have a different trigger (menus that hide animal products) and a weaker safety motive.
The r/Celiac channels do not reach the new segment.
Anti-persona needs rework: allergy travelers may now be the secondary segment, not excluded.

caps.reason: New segment named without context, trigger or channel; treated as unnamed until described

openQuestions: Describe the vegan traveler's worst meal abroad. What did they do?
Where do fifty of them talk to each other, and can you post there?

what.summary: Photo of a menu to dish cards with allergen flags for the user's profile, plus a local-language question card

ratings.rationale: MenuLens turns a photo of a menu into dish cards that say what each dish is, its main ingredients, and which of the user's allergens it may contain, then gives a phrase in the local language to confirm with staff. One photo, one answer, one question to ask.

Four features with acceptance criteria: allergy profile setup (REQ-001), menu photo to dish cards with flags (REQ-002), local-language confirmation card (REQ-003), cache of the last 20 scanned menus for offline re-reading (REQ-004).

Cut from v1 (DEC-003): dish recommendations and ranking, restaurant reviews, social sharing, favorites sync across devices, live camera translation, fully offline recognition. Google Lens remains the right tool for a traveler who only needs literal translation.

The user brings an allergy profile, a destination language and a camera. Business rule: a flag is a warning to confirm, never a clearance. Profile edge cases (multiple severe allergies, cross-contamination) are recorded as EDGE-003 and EDGE-004.

caps.reason: Cleared in turn 5: four features and a named anti-scope list

what.notes: Needs review after DEC-005: the allergy flags and the confirm-with-staff flow were designed for the previous beachhead.

which.summary: Mobile web app installed to the home screen; native deferred until retention is shown

ratings.rationale: DEC-001: a mobile web app with camera access and add-to-home-screen. Rejected: native iOS and Android for v1 (store review and two codebases in six weeks), a Telegram bot (no camera flow), a desktop site (wrong moment).
The traveler already has the phone out to photograph the menu. A link on the home screen that opens the camera matches that moment with no store download on hotel Wi-Fi.

Restaurants abroad mean roaming data and basements with one bar of signal. Images are compressed on the device before upload, results are cached, and the app degrades to the cached menus when offline (EDGE-002). Large text and labeled controls for one-handed use at a table.
One vision model API behind a thin server. No restaurant data, maps or payment APIs in v1. Provider choice is open until EXP-002 measures accuracy and latency.

caps.reason: Cleared in turn 6: web app chosen over native

whether.summary: Provisional 0.012 USD per scan against a 4.99 USD trip pass; allergen liability handled as a confirm-with-staff flow, not a clearance

ratings.rationale: ASM-002: one scan is one image plus about 1,500 output tokens, roughly 0.012 USD at the provider's listed vision pricing as of 2026-10 (needs re-verification before launch). At 12 scans a trip that is about 0.14 USD against a 4.99 USD pass. Monthly model cost at 100, 1,000 and 10,000 active users with one trip each: about 14, 140 and 1,400 USD, before hosting.
Scan latency of 6 to 10 seconds at a table is tolerable once, painful three times. Handwritten and chalkboard menus fail often (EDGE-001). Provider rate limits at launch are untested.

RISK-001: allergen flags are informational, never a clearance. Every card carries "confirm with staff" and the local-language question. Photos are processed and not stored. Issues to investigate before launch: consumer-protection wording for health information in the user's jurisdiction (Australia) and the EU for European users, and the model provider's terms on food images. Owner: the builder, before the first fifty users.

EDGE-001 handwritten menu, EDGE-002 no connectivity, EDGE-003 cross-contamination invisible on a menu, EDGE-004 user with several severe allergies who distrusts any flag. Each has a product response and a remaining exposure.

caps.reason: Cleared in turn 8: cost per scan and per trip estimated

whether.notes: Needs review after DEC-005: the allergy flags and the confirm-with-staff flow were designed for the previous beachhead.

when.summary: 15 hours a week for six weeks: 48-hour proof of concept, MVP in five weeks, one week of buffer before the trip

ratings.rationale: Solo builder, about 15 hours a week (weeknights and one weekend day) for six weeks until departure. Comfortable with web frontends and a small Node server. No budget beyond model calls and a 20 USD hosting plan.

TASK-001: within 48 hours of effort, photograph ten real menus from the user's last trip and get dish cards with a hardcoded allergy profile. Observe accuracy against a native speaker's reading (EXP-002).

MVP by the end of week five, one week of buffer before departure. Done means REQ-001 to REQ-004 pass their acceptance criteria on the builder's phone and two allergy travelers from r/Celiac have used it on a real menu photo.

Behind by the end of week three: drop the offline cache (REQ-004) first, then the confirmation card (REQ-003). Never drop the allergen flags. Timing matters because the trip is the first real test and the next one is months away.

caps.reason: Cleared in turn 10: four features on a web app fit 75 hours with a cut line

sources.title: Conversation with the user, turns 1 to 11
sources.limitations: Self-reported. The user is the beachhead persona, which helps the detail and biases the sample.

sources.title: Three r/Celiac threads about eating out in Japan, pasted by the user
sources.limitations: Shows that the problem is discussed and how people work around it. Does not show willingness to pay or market size.

personas.title: Allergy traveler
personas.situation: English speaker with celiac disease or a severe allergy, 2 or more trips a year to countries whose script they cannot read, already carries a printed allergy card
personas.outcome: Order a meal with confidence that it does not contain their allergen, and confirm it with staff in their language
personas.workaround: Google Lens for literal translation, printed cards, packaged food
personas.trigger: Booking a trip to a non-Latin-script country
objections: Can I trust a flag with my health
personas.firstValue: First scan shows a dish they would not have risked, flagged, with the question to ask

personas.title: Blind-ordering foodie and the hotel business traveler
personas.situation: Enjoys ordering without knowing, or eats where English menus exist
personas.reason: Neither has the allergen pain. Both would judge the product on recommendations and reviews, which are out of scope.

edges.title: Handwritten or chalkboard menu
edges.frequency: common in Italy and Japan izakaya
edges.response: Show a confidence state per card. Below the threshold, show the local-language question card only and say the menu could not be read.
edges.test: Given a photo the model cannot parse, when scanned, then no dish cards appear and the question card and an honest message do.

edges.title: No connectivity at the table
edges.frequency: frequent in basements and rural areas
edges.response: Keep the last 20 scanned menus and the question cards available offline. Compress images before upload so one bar is enough when there is signal.
edges.test: Given airplane mode, when the app opens, then cached menus and question cards are readable.

edges.title: Cross-contamination is invisible on a menu
edges.impact: A dish with no flagged ingredient can still be unsafe (shared fryer, soy sauce with wheat)
edges.response: Every card says that flags are a warning to confirm, not a clearance. The question card asks about preparation, not only ingredients.
edges.test: Given any dish card, then the confirm-with-staff line and the preparation question are present.

edges.title: Several severe allergies and low trust in any app
edges.response: Profile supports multiple allergens. Cards show the ingredient that triggered the flag, so the user can judge it, not only a red icon.
edges.test: Given a profile with three allergens, when a dish contains two, then both ingredients are named on the card.

decisions.title: Mobile web app first, native deferred
decisions.rationale: Six weeks, one builder, two platforms otherwise. Camera access from the browser is enough. Native reconsidered when retention after two trips is known.

decisions.title: Beachhead is the allergy traveler, not all travelers
decisions.rationale: Sharpest pain, reachable communities, the builder is one of them.

decisions.title: No recommendations, reviews, sharing, favorites sync, live translation or offline recognition in v1
decisions.rationale: None of them reduces allergen risk. Each adds a week.

decisions.title: Price as a trip pass at 4.99 USD with a yearly option
decisions.rationale: Matches how the segment buys travel tools. Untested.

decisions.title: Beachhead changes to vegetarians and vegans traveling abroad
decisions.rationale: At turn 12 the user said two friends who are vegan asked for it and that the allergy market felt too narrow. This is a new hypothesis, not evidence, so Who is re-rated and every record that depended on the allergy persona is flagged for review.
alternatives: Keep the allergy beachhead and add vegetarians as a second segment

requirements.title: Allergy profile
requirements.outcome: The user records one or more allergens and dietary rules once
acceptance: Given a new user, when they open the app, then they can select allergens from a list and add a free-text rule before the first scan
Given a saved profile, when the app reopens, then the profile is present without sign-in

requirements.title: Menu photo to dish cards with allergen flags
requirements.outcome: One photo becomes a list of dishes the user can judge
acceptance: Given a legible printed menu photo, when scanned, then each dish shows its name, a one-line description, main ingredients and a flag per matching allergen within 15 seconds
Given a flag, then the ingredient that caused it is named on the card

requirements.title: Local-language confirmation card
requirements.outcome: The user can ask staff about ingredients and preparation
acceptance: Given a dish card, when tapped, then a card in the destination language asks whether the dish contains the user's allergens and how it is prepared, with a transliteration

requirements.title: Offline cache of recent menus
requirements.outcome: Past scans are readable without signal
acceptance: Given airplane mode, when the app opens, then the last 20 scanned menus and their question cards are readable

risks.title: A flagged-safe dish harms a user
risks.mitigation: Flags are warnings, never clearances. Confirm-with-staff on every card. Preparation question included. Wording for health information to be investigated in Australia and the EU before launch.
risks.exposure: Residual. The app cannot see the kitchen.

risks.title: The model invents ingredients
risks.mitigation: Confidence state per card. Accuracy test against a native speaker on ten real menus before anyone else uses it.

risks.title: Vision pricing changes or rate limits bite
risks.mitigation: Re-verify pricing before launch. Thin server so the provider can be swapped.
risks.exposure: Cost per trip could double and still be under 0.30 USD.

assumptions.title: Allergy travelers will pay 4.99 USD for a trip pass
assumptions.implication: If false, the yearly option or a free tier with a scan limit is the fallback.

assumptions.title: One scan costs about 0.012 USD and a trip takes about 12 scans
assumptions.implication: If cost is 5 times higher the trip pass still covers it. Pricing is provisional and dated 2026-10.

experiments.title: Landing page and waitlist posted in r/Celiac and one Facebook group
experiments.measure: Sign-ups and replies to a 4.99 USD price question
experiments.decisionRule: Under 25 sign-ups means the channel or the pitch is wrong. Revisit Who before building REQ-003.

experiments.title: Ten real menus scored against a native speaker
experiments.measure: Dishes correctly identified, allergens correctly flagged, latency per scan
experiments.decisionRule: Under 80 percent correct flags means the core loop is not safe to ship. Stop or change approach.
